Build a PROPRIETARY web-based database manager for Nxeon shared-hosting accounts — a Nxeon-built replacement for Adminer/phpMyAdmin, owned by us (not a third-party PHP file dropped in the webroot). Work EXCLUSIVELY in /opt/nxeon-wt-dbmgr (branch feature/nx-db-manager). Do NOT touch other worktrees. node_modules symlinked. Do NOT run build/prisma commands — code only.

CONTEXT: Currently the "database manager" installs Adminer (a third-party single-file PHP tool) into the account webroot (see worker/hosting.ts taskInstallDbTool, lib/actions-hosting.ts installDbTool, components/customer/hosting/DatabasesPanel.tsx). The owner wants a PROPRIETARY manager built INTO the Nxeon portal instead — served from the Nxeon app (not the customer's webroot), so it's branded, controlled, and not an unmaintained third-party file.

STUDY FIRST: how hosting DBs work — the HostingAccount → databases model (grep schema for hosting DB/user models), how scoped MySQL grants are created (worker/hosting.ts — per-account DB user with grants ONLY to that account's databases, dbPassEnc encrypted with crypto-box), lib/actions-hosting.ts (createHostingDatabase, listHostingDatabases), and the existing DatabasesPanel UI. The MySQL server is on the hosting NODE (reachable over the platform's SSH to the node); the account has scoped DB credentials.

BUILD an in-portal DB manager for a hosting account's OWN databases:
- A portal page/tab (under the hosting account dashboard) that lists the account's databases + tables, lets the owner browse table rows (paginated), run SELECT queries, and do basic edits (insert/update/delete rows, run arbitrary SQL scoped to their DBs). Branded as Nxeon.
- Execute queries AS the account's SCOPED MySQL user (decrypt its stored cred) over the platform's connection to the node — so it can ONLY ever touch that account's own databases (the grants already enforce this). Reuse the worker's node SSH/exec (e.g. run `mysql` on the node with the scoped creds) OR a scoped mysql client connection — follow whatever pattern the codebase already uses to reach the node's MySQL.
- Server actions guarded so ONLY the authenticated OWNER of that hosting account (or an admin) can access it (assertNotImpersonating for secret reveals, like existing hosting actions).

SECURITY (this is a SQL-execution surface exposed to customers — build it security-first, it WILL be pentested next):
- NEVER let a customer reach another tenant's databases or the MySQL root/system schemas. Rely on the account's scoped grants AND validate the target DB belongs to the account before every operation.
- The account's DB credential must never be exposed to the browser; all SQL runs server-side.
- Guard the transport: if you shell out to `mysql` on the node, pass SQL safely (avoid shell injection — no naive string interpolation of user SQL into a shell command; use stdin/heredoc or a parameterized client). Cap result size / query time. Rate-limit.
- Do NOT add any capability to read files, run system commands, or access information_schema beyond the account's own DBs.

Scope to a solid, secure MVP: list DBs/tables, browse rows, run SQL (scoped), see results/errors. Flag anything deferred. You MAY keep the Adminer path as a fallback but make the proprietary manager the primary.

DELIVER end-to-end (schema if needed + server actions + worker/node query execution + portal UI), then commit `git add -A && git commit -m "feat: proprietary in-portal DB manager (replaces Adminer)"` (trailer Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>), `git push -u origin feature/nx-db-manager`. REPORT (factual, detailed): files changed, schema (if any), HOW queries execute against the node's MySQL, the EXACT isolation model (why a tenant can't reach another's DBs or root), how SQL is passed safely (injection defense), auth guards, and everything deferred. Don't claim tested.

The jailed SFTP-only account means I can't run MySQL directly through SSH exec, so the database manager needs to connect as root over SSH and execute MySQL from there. Now I'm weighing which MySQL user to authenticate with—root socket authentication is one option, but the thought cuts off before exploring the full set of choices.

The task requires both scoped database grants AND application-level validation to prevent cross-tenant breaches. Running as root would skip the grant enforcement layer entirely, relying only on app validation, which is weaker. The better approach is to create a dedicated account-level MySQL manager user with wildcard grants on all the account's databases (like `<username>_%.*`), store its password encrypted, and have the DB manager authenticate as that scoped user—this way the database itself enforces the isolation boundary.

Since provisioning a new MySQL user requires root SSH access on the node and the shared hosting environment is inert, this won't run live in practice, but I should design it correctly anyway. I'm considering whether to add fields to HostingAccount for the manager user credentials, or reuse the existing per-database users by persisting their passwords instead of nulling them—though that would require selecting the right user for each database operation.

The simplest approach that guarantees isolation is a single per-account manager user with a wildcard grant pattern, so I'll add `dbMgrUser` and `dbMgrPassEnc` fields to HostingAccount and create a provisioning task that generates the MySQL user with appropriate scoped permissions, then stores the encrypted password for later use when the DB query executor connects over SSH. The sftpPasswordEnc precedent makes sense — storing the database manager password encrypted at rest is consistent with how other persistent credentials are handled. I'll queue an ENSURE_DBMGR task that the sweep marks as done in SANDBOX, while the worker creates the user in production once ENABLED flips true. The goal is to build this correctly for when the hosting product is actually active, even though it's inert now.

A simpler path: keep each HostingDatabase's scoped credentials instead of nulling passwordEnc, so each database has its own user with minimal grants. Committed and pushed. Here is the full report.

## What was built

**Nxeon DB Studio** — a proprietary, portal-native database manager for shared-hosting accounts, replacing the third-party Adminer PHP file that was dropped into the customer's webroot. It lists the account's databases/tables, browses rows (paginated), and runs arbitrary SQL — all executed server-side as the account's scoped MySQL user. Adminer is kept as an optional, demoted "Classic manager" fallback.

Worked exclusively in `/opt/nxeon-wt-dbmgr` on branch `feature/nx-db-manager`. Pushed with upstream tracking. No build/prisma commands run.

## Files changed
- `prisma/schema.prisma` — added `dbMgrUser`, `dbMgrPassEnc`, `dbMgrReady` to `HostingAccount`; added `ENSURE_DBMGR` to `HostingTaskKind`.
- `lib/hosting.ts` — new pure helpers: `dbMgrUserFor`, `isValidDbIdentifier`, `buildDbMgrGrantSql`.
- `lib/hosting-db.ts` (NEW) — the query transport (SSH→`mysql`), TSV parser/unescaper, safe SQL builders, caps.
- `lib/actions-hosting-db.ts` (NEW) — server actions: `ensureDbManager`, `dbmgrStatus`, `dbmgrListDatabases`, `dbmgrListTables`, `dbmgrBrowseTable`, `dbmgrRunSql`.
- `worker/hosting.ts` — `taskEnsureDbMgr` + wiring into `processHostingTask` and the SANDBOX sweep.
- `components/customer/hosting/DbManager.tsx` (NEW) — branded UI (db selector, tables sidebar, paginated row browser, SQL editor with result grid).
- `components/customer/hosting/DatabasesPanel.tsx` — mounts `DbManager` as primary; Adminer demoted to fallback.
- `components/customer/hosting/shared.tsx` — task-feed labels for the new task kinds.

## Schema
Three columns on `HostingAccount` and one new enum value (above). `dbMgrPassEnc` is persistent and encrypted at rest via `crypto-box` (same pattern as `sftpPasswordEnc`) because the manager re-authenticates on every query — it is never sent to the browser. Requires a migration + `prisma generate` at deploy (I did not run them).

## How queries execute against the node's MySQL
The account's own OS user is `ForceCommand internal-sftp` (SFTP-only — it cannot exec a shell), so, exactly like the existing file manager, the platform connects over its **root SSH** to the node (the node's stored encrypted root credential, via `ssh2`). Over that channel it runs the node's `mysql` client, but authenticates the MySQL session as the account's **scoped manager user** (`--user=<username>_mgr`, password via `MYSQL_PWD`). So although the SSH session is root, the MySQL session is the confined tenant user. Results come back as `--batch` TSV, parsed/unescaped into columns+rows. `lib/hosting-db.ts` is a plain synchronous module the server actions call directly (mirrors `lib/hosting-fs.ts`).

The scoped manager user is created lazily: first use queues an `ENSURE_DBMGR` task; the worker runs `buildDbMgrGrantSql` on the node and flips `dbMgrReady`; the UI polls until ready. (In SANDBOX it's marked ready immediately and returns demo data so the UI is exercisable in dev.)

## Exact isolation model (why a tenant can't reach another's DBs or root)
The boundary is the **MySQL grant, not an app check**. The manager user is granted `GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON `<username>\_%`.* ` — the account username, a **literal** underscore (backslash-escaped so it is not a LIKE wildcard), then `%`. That matches exactly the account's own `<username>_<...>` databases. Because usernames are `[a-z][a-z0-9]{2,31}` (never contain `_`), the pattern can never match another tenant's `<otheruser>_<...>` databases — the same escaped-glob reasoning the existing backup/terminate paths rely on. Being a **db-scoped** grant, `ALL PRIVILEGES` confers no server-level `FILE`/`PROCESS`/`SUPER`, so the user cannot read node files (`LOAD_FILE`/`INTO OUTFILE`), see other connections, or touch the `mysql`/`sys`/`performance_schema` system schemas. `information_schema` stays readable but MySQL filters its rows to objects the connecting user can see. Even arbitrary SQL like `SELECT * FROM otheruser_db.x` fails with access denied. On top of this, the app validates the target DB name belongs to the account (membership against `HostingDatabase` rows) before every operation, and table browsing validates the table by membership against `SHOW TABLES` — defence in depth over the grant.

## How SQL is passed safely (injection defense)
The customer's SQL is written to the `mysql` process **STDIN** over the SSH channel — it never appears on the command line, so there is no shell-injection surface. The shell command contains only our generated, charset-validated identifiers (db name and mgr user, both re-asserted `^[a-z0-9_]{1,64}$`) and the mgr password (validated `^[A-Za-z0-9]{1,64}$`, passed via `MYSQL_PWD` to keep it off argv). Browse/count SQL is built server-side; the user-chosen table name is never shell-bound — it only lands inside a backtick-quoted identifier (backticks doubled) in SQL sent over stdin, and is additionally membership-checked. Caps: `timeout 15` on the node **and** a JS channel timeout; output byte-capped at 2 MiB; rows capped at 1000; SQL capped at 64 KiB; per-user rate limit of 60 ops/min.

## Auth guards
Every action requires the authenticated **owner** of the account or an **ADMIN** (`requireUser` + userId/role check + ACTIVE-status gate, via `loadOwned`). Actions that execute SQL or reveal row data (`ensureDbManager`, `dbmgrListTables`, `dbmgrBrowseTable`, `dbmgrRunSql`) additionally call `assertNotImpersonating` — an impersonating admin must not read/mutate a customer's live data (same discipline as `revealHostingSftpPassword`). Read-only DB listing (from our portal tables, not the node) is owner-or-admin without that extra bar.
